entities.name: Francesco Moricotti Prignani
entities.label: Person
entities.summary:
Francesco Moricotti Prignani (also spelled Prignano), born in Italy in an unknown year, ascended to significant ecclesiastical power during the tumultuous Western Schism, dying on February 14, 1394. His career epitomized the influence of nepotism within the late medieval papacy, as he owed his cardinalate to his uncle, Pope Urban VI. As a cardinal-nephew, Prignani played a direct role in the initial, volatile phase of the Schism, serving as a key loyalist to the Roman line of popes and participating in crucial diplomatic and administrative functions that sought to legitimize Urban VI's claim against the Avignon antipopes. His elevation in 1378, alongside 15 other cardinals, was a deliberate move by Urban VI to consolidate power and establish a new college of cardinals loyal to him, following the defection of most cardinals who had elected him.

Moricotti Prignani's ecclesiastical career began with his appointment as Archbishop of Acerenza in 1378, quickly followed by his elevation to Cardinal-Priest of Sant'Eusebio by Pope Urban VI on September 18, 1378. This rapid ascent occurred just months after the outbreak of the Western Schism, making him an immediate participant in the deep divisions fracturing the Catholic Church. He subsequently held the prestigious position of Camerlengo of the Sacred College of Cardinals from 1380 until his death, a role that placed him in charge of the college's finances and temporal administration. During this period, he was instrumental in the curial operations of the Roman obedience, helping to manage the financial and logistical challenges posed by the Schism, including the need to secure new sources of revenue and maintain diplomatic relations with kingdoms loyal to Rome.

historicalSignificance.significanceNarrative: Francesco Moricotti Prignani was a significant administrative figure within the Roman obedience during the early decades of the Western Schism, his role as Camerlengo providing vital financial and organizational stability to one of the two competing papal lines.
